Classical Symmetries and Painlevé Analysis for the (1+3)- Kudryashov-Sinelshchikov Equation

Amlan K Halder Address: School of Sciences, Woxsen University, Hyderabad 502345, Telangana, India Email address: amlanhalder1@gmail.com , Rajeswari Seshadri Address: Department of Mathematics, Pondicherry University, Puducherry - 605014, India Email address: seshadrirajeswari@gmail.com , A Paliathanasis* Address: *Corresponding Author. Address: Institute for Systems Science, Durban University of Technology, PO Box 1334, Durban 4000, South Africa Address: School for Data Science and Computational Thinking, Stellenbosch University, Stellenbosch, 7602, South Afrika Address: Departamento de Matemáticas, Universidad Católica del Norte, Avda. Angamos 0610, Casilla 1280 Antofagasta, Chile Address: School of Sciences, Woxsen University, Hyderabad 502345, Telangana, India Email address: anpaliat@phys.uoa.gr and PGL Leach Address: School of Mathematics, Statistics and Computer Science, University of KwaZulu-Natal, Durban, South Africa and Email address: leachp@ukzn.ac.za
Date: 27:10:2024
Abstract.

The integrability of the Kudryashov-Sinelshchikov equation in (1+3)−(1+3)- dimension is detected using its point symmetries and the Singularity analysis method. The symmetries mostly points to the existence of infinite-dimensional Lie algebra with the presence of mostly arbitrary functions. The reduction process is initiated by considering these arbitrary functions in the general symmetry vectors. For certain functions, trivial solutions for the general parent equation is obtained whereas for some of the functions, the reductions does not yield an unmitigated result. Finally, a positive result is listed for one of the arbitrary function, for which the singularity analysis method is employed to study the Painlevé property. The resultant PDE happens to be a fourth-order equation and its approval of the Painlevé property hints at the integrability of the Kudryashov-Sinelshchikov equation in the general case.

Key words and phrases: 
Symmetry analysis; Similarity solutions; Closed-form solution; Singularity analysis
1991 Mathematics Subject Classification
MSC 2010: 35B06,34A05, 34A34, 34C14, 22E60, 35C05, 35C07

1. Introduction

In 20122012, Kudryashov and Sinelshchikov [16] introduced certain equation discussing the phenomenon of nonlinear waves in the liquid medium with gas bubbles. The authors cited the importance of the long weakly nonlinear waves as computationally feasible and efficient. Enormous amount of work which is focussed on the derivation of exact and special type solutions have been done by considering the parameters which appears in the original equation to be of particular value or of functions of the variable tt [1, 14, 17, 19, 23]. It is to be noted here that the equation, in general, is considered to be not integrable, as it fails to pass the necessary requirements of the Painlev é test [20, 21, 22]. This forms the basis of our work.

In this paper, the symmetries of the equation by considering the various parameters which appears in the original equation [16] are computed and certain reductions are also listed. Our important observation is one of the reduction with respect to an arbitrary function symmetry, which leads to a (1+2)−(1+2)- dimensional equation of fourth-order and is deduced to be integrable by passing the Painlevé test. Now, this is quite peculiar, since the order of the parent equation is also four, this could point to the possibility of integrability for the parent equation. This result is mentioned in case 66 and forms the main result of our work.

The (1+3)−(1+3)- dimensional equation is presented as [16],

(1.1) (μ3μ1+1)ux​xu(t,x,y,z)+ut​x+μ2​ux​x​x​x2​μ1+(μ3μ1+1)ux−2μ4​ux​x​x2​μ1+12μ52uy​y+12μ6uz​z=0,\left(\frac{\text{$\mu_{3}$}}{\text{$\mu_{1}$}}+1\right)u_{xx}u(t,x,y,z)+u_{tx}+\frac{\text{$\mu_{2}$}u_{xxxx}}{2\text{$\mu_{1}$}}+\left(\frac{\text{$\mu_{3}$}}{\text{$\mu_{1}$}}+1\right)u_{x}{}^{2}-\frac{\text{$\mu_{4}$}u_{xxx}}{2\text{$\mu_{1}$}}+\frac{1}{2}\text{$\mu_{5}$}^{2}u_{yy}+\frac{1}{2}\text{$\mu_{6}$}u_{zz}=0,

where uu represent the density of the gas bubbles in the liquid medium and the parameters μ1,μ2,μ3,μ4,μ5,μ6\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\mu_{3},\mu_{4},\mu_{5},\mu_{6} represent various constant terms describing various physical phenomenon[14]. The structure of the paper is as follows.

In Section 2 we present the Lie symmetries for the (1+3)\left(1+3\right)-Kudryashov-Sinelshchikov equation. We employ the Lie symmetries to construct similarity transformations and perform reductions. Then we apply the singularity analysis to investigate if the reduced equations possess the Painlevé property and if the solution can be expressed in terms of Laurent expansions. In Section 3, we discuss and approach on how to write an equivalent system which has a finite number of symmetries. We do that by introducing a new dependent variable, from where we can calculate a finite-dimensional Lie algebra which leads to the same family of similarity transformations as the infinite-dimensional Lie algebra. Finally, in Section 4 we draw our conclusions.

2. Symmetries of Equation (1.1)

The group analysis of differential equations mainly deals with the procedure of obtaining generators of certain transformations which tends to preserve the properties of the differential equations. These generators of transformations represents the underlying algebraic structures of the differential equations under study. Finite representations of these generators leads to proper reductions and possible solutions of the original differential equations and the infinite representations needs proper analysis and treatment to obtain suitable reductions, for more details we refer the reader to [3, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 15].

The general symmetry vector of equation (1.1) is

3. From infinity to a finite Lie algebra

We found before that equation (1.1) admits an infinite-dimensional Lie algebra. The coefficients of the Lie symmetries are factors of tt. There are four vector fields which related to the four functions b⁡(t),c⁡(t)b\left(t\right),~c\left(t\right), d1​(t)d_{1}\left(t\right) and d2​(t)d_{2}\left(t\right). They are

(3.1) Γ2=duμ1​(−y​c′′​(t))μ52​(μ1+μ3)−dx​(y​(c′​(t))μ52)+dy​(c​(t))\Gamma_{2}=\frac{\text{du$\mu_{1}$}\left(-y\text{c}^{\prime\prime}(t)\right)}{\text{$\mu_{5}$}^{2}(\text{$\mu_{1}$}+\text{$\mu_{3}$})}-\text{dx}\left(\frac{y\left(\text{c}^{\prime}(t)\right)}{\text{$\mu_{5}$}^{2}}\right)+\text{dy}\left(\text{c}(t)\right)
(3.2) Γ3=duμ1​(−z​d1′′​(t))μ6​(μ1+μ3)−dx​(z​(−d1′​(t))μ6)+dz​(d1​(t))\Gamma_{3}=\frac{\text{du}\text{$\mu_{1}$}\left(-z\text{$d_{1}$}^{\prime\prime}(t)\right)}{\text{$\mu_{6}$}(\text{$\mu_{1}$}+\text{$\mu_{3}$})}-\text{dx}\left(\frac{z\left(-\text{$d_{1}$}^{\prime}(t)\right)}{\text{$\mu_{6}$}}\right)+\text{dz}(\text{$d_{1}$}(t))

From the vector fields we can calculate the infinitesimal transformations.

Indeed, the vector field Γ1\Gamma_{1} provides the infinitesimal transformation

x¯=x+ε​b​(t),u¯=u+ε​μ1​b′​(t)(μ1+μ3).\bar{x}=x+\varepsilon b\left(t\right),~\bar{u}=u+\varepsilon\frac{\text{$\mu_{1}$}b^{\prime}(t)}{(\text{$\mu_{1}$}+\text{$\mu_{3}$})}.

The arbitrance of the function b⁡(t)b\left(t\right) is due to the existence of the ut​xu_{tx} term in equation (1.1). This term means that every function u=u⁡(t)u=u\left(t\right) is a solution for equation (1.1). That is exactly the original of the arbitrance of the above functions.

Let us now introduce the new dependent function v=utv=u_{t}, such equation (1.1) to be expressed as the following system

(3.4) (μ3μ1+1)ux​xu+vx+μ2​ux​x​x​x2​μ1+(μ3μ1+1)ux−2μ4​ux​x​x2​μ1+12μ52uy​y+12μ6uz​z\displaystyle\left(\frac{\text{$\mu_{3}$}}{\text{$\mu_{1}$}}+1\right)u_{xx}u+v_{x}+\frac{\text{$\mu_{2}$}u_{xxxx}}{2\text{$\mu_{1}$}}+\left(\frac{\text{$\mu_{3}$}}{\text{$\mu_{1}$}}+1\right)u_{x}{}^{2}-\frac{\text{$\mu_{4}$}u_{xxx}}{2\text{$\mu_{1}$}}+\frac{1}{2}\text{$\mu_{5}$}^{2}u_{yy}+\frac{1}{2}\text{$\mu_{6}$}u_{zz} =\displaystyle= 0,\displaystyle 0,
(3.5) v−ut\displaystyle v-u_{t} =\displaystyle= 0.\displaystyle 0.

The Lie symmetries of the later system are

X1=∂t,X2=∂x,X3=∂y,X4=∂z and X5=μ52z∂z−μ6y∂z.X_{1}=\partial_{t}~,~X_{2}=\partial_{x},~X_{3}=\partial_{y},~X_{4}=\partial_{z}\text{ and }X_{5}=\mu_{5}^{2}z\partial_{z}-\mu_{6}y\partial_{z}.

The vector fields X1,X2,X3X_{1},~X_{2},~X_{3} and X4X_{4} are translations and X5X_{5} is a rotation in the two-dimensional place {y,z}\left\{y,z\right\}. These vector fields follows from the generic vector field Γ\Gamma of equation (1.1) by assuming that b⁡(t)=b0,c⁡(t)=c0b\left(t\right)=b_{0},~c\left(t\right)=c_{0}, d1​(t)=d10d_{1}\left(t\right)=d_{1}^{0} and d2​(t)=d20d_{2}\left(t\right)=d_{2}^{0}.

Consequently, the application of these vector fields for the derivation of similarity transformations leads to the same form of transformations as these studied in the previous section. Nevertheless the application of the vector fields provides less arbitrary functions, thus less calculations.

4. Conclusion

In this work, certain trivial reductions and hence the solutions of the Kudryashov-Sinelshchikov equation in (1+3)−(1+3)- dimension are listed. The important observation is a reduction with one of the symmetry vector with arbitrary function. The reduced equation in (1+2)−(1+2)- dimension possesses a series solution with required number of arbitrary constants and hence passes the Painlevé test.

This result can be easily connected to the parent equation which is in (1+3)−(1+3)- dimension and of fourth-order, hence also fingers to the integrability of equation (1.1).

Further study involving computation of various nonclassical symmetry is under study.
